did_you_know.text: Did you know? The chapter opens by introducing Joel son of Pethuel and stating that its message is the word of the LORD delivered to him.
Did you know? Joel addresses the elders and all the inhabitants of the land, asking them to consider whether anything like this disaster has happened in their days or in the days of their ancestors.

Did you know? The devastation is described as a succession of four pests—the cutting locust, the swarming locust, the hopping locust, and the destroying locust—with each one consuming what the previous one left behind.
Did you know? The calamity also affects wine drinkers, because the new wine—the juice of the grapes—has been cut off from their mouths.
Did you know? The damage to agriculture is described in detail: the vine and the fig tree have been struck, their branches stripped bare, and their shoots turned white.
Did you know? The shortage affects the main field crops: the grain has been ruined, the new wine has dried up, and the olive oil has withered.
Did you know? The priests are called to put on sackcloth and mourn, because the lack of produce prevents the grain offering and drink offering from being presented in the house of the LORD.
Did you know? Joel calls for a fast to be consecrated, an assembly to be proclaimed, and the elders and all the inhabitants of the land to be gathered at the house of the LORD to cry out to him.
Did you know? The shortage is not limited to the fields: the seeds rot beneath their clods, the storehouses lie desolate, and the granaries are destroyed because the grain has dried up.
Did you know? At the end of the chapter, even the wild animals join the description of the distress: the watercourses have dried up, and fire has consumed the pastures of the wilderness.
